rm_c1_prompting.question_text: Which CRAF element is missing from this prompt: "Write an email to a prospect about our export financing products"?

options.label: A
options.text: Context — there is no information about who the prospect is or their situation

options.label: B
options.text: Role — the AI has not been told what professional is asking

options.label: C
options.text: Action — the task (write an email) is not specified

options.label: D
options.text: Format — the email structure has not been defined

rm_c1_prompting.explanation: The prompt has an implied Role (an EDC employee), an Action (write an email), and an implied Format (email). What it completely lacks is Context — who is the prospect, what do they export, what is their current situation? Without context the AI will write a generic email applicable to no one in particular.

rm_c1_prompting.question_text: A well-structured CRAF prompt should tell the AI:

options.label: A
options.text: The client context, the role to speak from, exactly what to produce, and how to format the output

options.label: B
options.text: The client's full legal name, credit history, and account balance

options.label: C
options.text: Your personal background, your manager's name, and today's date

options.label: D
options.text: The AI tool version you are using and your preferred language

rm_c1_prompting.explanation: CRAF = Context (who/what/situation) + Role (voice the AI speaks from) + Action (specific deliverable) + Format (structure of output). Together these four elements give the AI everything it needs to produce output that is specific and directly usable in an RM workflow.

rm_c1_prompting.question_text: After using AI to draft a discovery brief, the best next step is:

options.label: A
options.text: Review it, remove anything inaccurate or generic, then use it

options.label: B
options.text: Send it to the client immediately to save time

options.label: C
options.text: Submit it to your manager for approval before using any AI output

options.label: D
options.text: Regenerate it with a different prompt until it looks exactly right

rm_c1_prompting.explanation: AI output is a starting point, not a final product. Reviewing and editing ensures accuracy and relevance before use. Sending unreviewed AI output to a client is a quality and trust risk. Regenerating indefinitely is inefficient. Manager approval is not the standard process for internal preparation documents.

rm_c1_prompting.question_text: Write a complete CRAF prompt to generate a one-page briefing document before your first discovery call with a new prospect.
rm_c1_prompting.scenario_text: Company: Shoreline Advisory Group Ltd., a financial advisory firm based in Vancouver with approximately $20M in annual revenues. They are planning to expand into the US market over the next 12 months and have not worked with EDC before. You are an RM preparing for a discovery call with their VP of Finance.

rm_c2_verification.question_text: An AI meeting recap says a client "committed to sending financials by Friday". Your notes say they "mentioned financials". What should you do before logging to C3?

options.label: A
options.text: Change 'committed' to 'mentioned' and add 'no firm deadline given'

options.label: B
options.text: Log it as written — the AI is usually reliable about commitments

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the financials reference entirely to avoid confusion

options.label: D
options.text: Email the client to ask if they recall making the commitment

rm_c2_verification.explanation: The difference between 'committed' and 'mentioned' is material. Logging a false commitment creates follow-up risk and erodes CRM data quality. The correct action is to correct the language to match what was actually said and note that no deadline was set.

rm_c2_verification.question_text: Which of these is NOT a reliable source for verifying an AI meeting recap?

options.label: A
options.text: Another AI-generated summary of the same call

options.label: B
options.text: Your handwritten notes taken during the call

options.label: C
options.text: A recorded transcript you reviewed manually

options.label: D
options.text: A follow-up email listing agreed action items

rm_c2_verification.explanation: Using one AI output to verify another does not add reliability — both could share the same underlying hallucination from the same audio source. Personal notes, manually reviewed transcripts, and follow-up emails are independent sources that provide genuine verification.

rm_c2_verification.question_text: The best format for a CRM activity note after a client call is:

options.label: A
options.text: Factual, present-tense bullets with confirmed commitments and clear next steps

options.label: B
options.text: A narrative paragraph that captures the tone and energy of the conversation

options.label: C
options.text: The full Copilot transcript pasted verbatim

options.label: D
options.text: A forward-looking interpretation of what the client probably wants next

rm_c2_verification.explanation: CRM notes are corporate memory. They should be factual, structured, and based only on what was confirmed — not speculative or narrative. A colleague or future RM reading the note should be able to understand the client's situation and next steps without having been on the call.

rm_c2_verification.question_text: The following AI-generated recap contains errors. Identify all errors and rewrite it as a corrected, CRM-ready activity note.
rm_c2_verification.scenario_text:
AI Recap: Call with Eastport Composites Ltd. — Jan 9, 2025. Attendees: Priya Nair (RM), Daniel Osei (CEO). Daniel confirmed they are closing a $5M export contract with a US buyer this quarter. He committed to sending the signed term sheet by Jan 13. The company wants to explore BCAP and PRI immediately. Follow-up call scheduled for Jan 16.

Priya's notes: Daniel = CFO not CEO. $5M contract still in negotiation, not confirmed. He said he might send term sheet — no date given. Interested in BCAP, PRI is new to him and he asked for more info. Follow-up call TBD.

rm_c3_data_safety.question_text: You want to use Copilot to draft an outreach email for a client whose $3.2M facility is expiring. The safest approach is:

options.label: A
options.text: Describe the client as 'a mid-market client with a facility expiring this quarter' without naming the amount or client

options.label: B
options.text: Include the exact facility amount so Copilot can write a more specific email

options.label: C
options.text: Include the client name but not the facility amount

options.label: D
options.text: Only use Copilot if the client has given verbal consent to share their data

rm_c3_data_safety.explanation: The safest prompt removes both the client identifier and the specific financial detail. The email can still be useful and personalized without these — Copilot does not need the exact figure to write an effective renewal message. Option C still identifies the client, which is non-public in combination with any relationship context.

rm_c3_data_safety.question_text: Which of the following C3 data fields is safe to include in a Copilot prompt without abstraction?

options.label: A
options.text: The client's industry sector (e.g., 'food processing')

options.label: B
options.text: The client's exact credit facility amount

options.label: C
options.text: A verbatim copy of your CRM relationship notes

options.label: D
options.text: The client's full legal name as it appears in C3

rm_c3_data_safety.explanation: Industry sector is typically publicly available information and does not identify the specific client or reveal confidential deal terms. The other options are all non-public: facility amount reveals deal terms, relationship notes are confidential observations, and the client's name combined with any relationship context is identifying.

rm_c3_data_safety.question_text: The "press release test" for AI prompts means:

options.label: A
options.text: Only include information that could appear in a public press release without causing a compliance issue

options.label: B
options.text: Ask your manager to review every AI prompt before you submit it

options.label: C
options.text: Only use AI tools that are approved by the communications department

options.label: D
options.text: Draft a press release first, then use it as context for your AI prompt

rm_c3_data_safety.explanation: The press release test is a quick mental check: if the information couldn't appear publicly without causing a compliance or confidentiality issue, it shouldn't go into an AI prompt. It's a fast, practical way to apply the public/non-public rule in real-time without needing to consult a policy document.

rm_c3_data_safety.question_text: Rewrite the following prompt so it is safe to use in Copilot. Remove or abstract all non-public information while keeping the prompt useful and specific enough to produce a usable email.
rm_c3_data_safety.scenario_text: Original prompt: 'I need to re-engage Cedar Valley Foods Ltd., a food processing company in Manitoba. They had a $2.8M BCAP facility that expired in September 2024. My CRM notes say they are exploring other lenders due to pricing concerns. Write me a re-engagement email that addresses pricing objections and emphasizes EDC's long-term partnership value.'

rm_c4_tool_fluency.question_text: You need to catch up on a 45-minute Teams meeting that happened while you were with another client. The meeting transcript is available. Which Copilot surface should you use?

options.label: A
options.text: Teams Copilot — it has direct access to the meeting transcript

options.label: B
options.text: Outlook Copilot — search for a follow-up email summarizing the meeting

options.label: C
options.text: Word Copilot — paste the transcript text and ask for a summary

options.label: D
options.text: Excel Copilot — structured data extraction works best for long meetings

rm_c4_tool_fluency.explanation: Teams Copilot is the only M365 surface with native access to Teams meeting transcripts. It can generate a summary, extract action items, and identify key decisions in seconds — without you manually copying or pasting anything. Outlook has no access to Teams transcripts, and Word/Excel Copilot would require manual effort to get the transcript in.

rm_c4_tool_fluency.question_text: You have a Copilot-generated meeting summary and want to turn it into a one-page structured briefing note for your manager. The best next step is:

options.label: A
options.text: Open Word and use Word Copilot to structure the summary into a briefing note format

options.label: B
options.text: Email the summary to yourself and use Outlook Copilot to reformat it

options.label: C
options.text: Paste it back into Teams chat and ask Teams Copilot to add headings

options.label: D
options.text: Log it directly into C3 — a meeting summary is already a usable format

rm_c4_tool_fluency.explanation: Word Copilot is the right surface for document structuring and drafting. It can take unstructured text (a meeting summary) and reformat it into a professional briefing note with headings, sections, and consistent structure. Outlook is for email; Teams is for meeting data; C3 is for CRM logs — none of these are designed for document formatting.

rm_c4_tool_fluency.question_text: In a multi-step Copilot workflow, the correct sequence for going from a missed Teams call to a follow-up email is:

options.label: A
options.text: Teams Copilot (recap) → Word Copilot (briefing note) → Outlook Copilot (draft email)

options.label: B
options.text: Outlook Copilot (summarize) → Word Copilot (structure) → Teams Copilot (send)

options.label: C
options.text: Excel Copilot (analyze) → Teams Copilot (share) → Outlook Copilot (draft)

options.label: D
options.text: SharePoint Copilot (search) → Teams Copilot (recap) → Word Copilot (summarize)

rm_c4_tool_fluency.explanation: The input type drives the starting surface: a Teams transcript starts in Teams. Structuring content into a document is Word's strength. Drafting outbound communication is Outlook's strength. The sequence follows the natural flow: extract information → structure it → communicate it.

rm_c4_tool_fluency.question_text: Describe a complete three-step M365 Copilot workflow for the following scenario.
rm_c4_tool_fluency.scenario_text:
You missed a Friday Teams call with a client about renewing their trade finance facility. The transcript is available in Teams. By noon on Monday you need to: (1) understand what was discussed and any commitments made, (2) prepare a one-page summary for your manager, and (3) send the client a follow-up email with clear next steps.

For each step, specify: which M365 Copilot surface you use, what prompt you write, and what the output is.

rm_c5_capstone.question_text: Before using AI to analyze a C3 export for a win-back program, the first step is:

options.label: A
options.text: Abstract all non-public fields — remove client names, round amounts, generalize sectors

options.label: B
options.text: Ask your manager for permission to upload the C3 data to Copilot

options.label: C
options.text: Use only the last contact date field since dates are not confidential

options.label: D
options.text: Run the analysis first, then redact sensitive output before sharing it

rm_c5_capstone.explanation: Abstraction must happen before any AI tool receives the data. Running the analysis first and redacting later does not fix the policy violation — the non-public data has already been processed by an unapproved surface. Option C is insufficient: last contact date combined with facility type can still identify a client in context.

rm_c5_capstone.question_text: A Copilot-generated outreach email includes a specific claim about a client interest rate that you never provided in your prompt. What should you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Delete the claim — it is likely hallucinated since you never provided that data

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the claim — Copilot probably accessed current market rate data

options.label: C
options.text: Call the client first to confirm whether the rate is accurate

options.label: D
options.text: Add a disclaimer saying the rate is approximate before sending

rm_c5_capstone.explanation: If you did not provide the rate data, the AI invented it. AI models do not have access to private client records — any specific figure that appears without being in the prompt is a hallucination. Sending a hallucinated financial claim to a client is both inaccurate and a compliance risk. Delete it and replace with a verified or general statement.

rm_c5_capstone.question_text: In a multi-step win-back workflow, the correct sequence is:

options.label: A
options.text: Abstract C3 data → analyze with Excel Copilot → draft with Outlook Copilot → verify before sending

options.label: B
options.text: Draft with Outlook Copilot → analyze with Excel → abstract data → verify and send

options.label: C
options.text: Export raw C3 data → summarize with Teams Copilot → draft with Outlook → send

options.label: D
options.text: Verify first → abstract → draft outreach → analyze results

rm_c5_capstone.explanation: Data safety comes first (abstract), then analysis (Excel), then communication drafting (Outlook), then verification before anything goes to a client. Running steps out of order — especially drafting before abstracting or sending before verifying — creates compliance and quality risks that are difficult to reverse.

rm_c5_capstone.question_text: Describe your complete AI-assisted win-back workflow for the scenario below.
rm_c5_capstone.scenario_text:
You have a C3 export of 8 lapsed clients in the food processing sector. You want to identify your top 3 priority targets and draft a personalized re-engagement email for each priority segment.

For each step of your workflow, describe: (1) which tool or Copilot surface you use, (2) what data preparation you perform before using it, (3) what prompt you write, and (4) what verification you perform before acting on the output.

Your workflow must address all four RM AI skill domains: data safety, prompting structure, tool selection, and output verification.
